tagline: Nineteen miles beside Seneca Lake, from Lodi to Watkins Glen
intro: The Seneca Lake Scenic Byway follows 19 miles along the lake’s southeastern side, connecting Lodi Point State Marine Park with Clute Park in Watkins Glen. On Route 414 through Hector, the road runs along the side of the lake valley, descending toward the water when driven south. New York’s Department of Transportation identifies scenic, historical, recreational and natural themes for the byway, highlighting gorges, waterfalls and agricultural production.

The road had several identities before becoming a scenic byway. The Watkins Glen-to-Ovid section became legislative Route 45 in 1911. Later numbered NY 44, the highway became NY 414 to avoid duplicating the number of the new U.S. 44. Community volunteers began working toward the scenic byway in the early 2000s, establishing and preserving its official New York State status. The organization remains entirely volunteer-run, continuing the work of the people who established the route’s identity as a scenic byway.

For a southbound drive, start with Lodi Point on the lake and Lodi village inland. Route 414 draws closer to the water through Hector toward Watkins Glen. Near the junction with Route 79, it reaches the foot of the valley beside the lake. Finish at Clute Park in Watkins Glen, the byway’s southern endpoint.

moments.title: Lodi
moments.text: Lodi Point was a freight stop as well as a passenger landing. After 1828, steamboats called there regularly, and warehouses handled coal, lime, salt, lumber, groceries and grain. By 1905 the commercial businesses had disappeared, although steamboat service continued into the early twentieth century. The state park occupies the lakeshore west of Lodi village. The village itself stands at the meeting of Routes 96A and 414, while Lodi Point projects into Seneca Lake. The byway takes the marine park as its northern endpoint. The Seneca Chief is believed to have stopped at Lodi Point during its inaugural voyage in 1828.

moments.title: Watkins Glen
moments.text: A checkered flag on Watkins Glen’s main street marks the original start-finish line of its road race. Resident Cameron Argetsinger organized the first Watkins Glen Sports Car Grand Prix in 1948, using public streets in and near the village. The 6.6-mile course passed through the village center. A crash killed a spectator in 1952; the race moved to a closed circuit of roads in 1953. A permanent racing facility opened in 1956, but the streets of the original course remain intact. The International Motor Racing Research Center opened in a public-library annex in 1999 to preserve motorsports history.

moments.title: Watkins Glen State Park
moments.text: Glen Creek cuts a narrow gorge 400 feet deep at Watkins Glen State Park. Glaciers deepened the Seneca valley, leaving the tributary stream hanging above it; the steeper descent created rapids and waterfalls where hard rock interrupted the creek. The visitor route has its own history of rebuilding. Floodwater destroyed bridges, railings and walkways in 1935, and the Civilian Conservation Corps rebuilt with low mortared stone walls and arches. That work was completed in 1938. The Gorge Trail follows 19 waterfalls, passing over, under and alongside them by way of bridges and more than 800 stone steps.
